slides.title: Chapter 2: How Bitcoin Works
slides.say: Chapter 1 asked what Bitcoin is; chapter 2 follows one payment - Alice pays Bob - all the way from her wallet to a buried block, and meets every moving part on the way. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2.
slides.concept: Transactions, the network, and the chain - one payment, followed all the way

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: Five parts, one payment followed all the way. The stories carry the why, the consoles carry the proof, and every slide number here is printed bottom-right as we pass it. A question to think about is this: which part do you expect to be hardest? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in every section.
slides.concept: Five parts, one payment followed all the way through

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: Each question on this slide is one the chapter answers, from the parts of a transaction to what a confirmation buys. We return to every one of them as the chapter proceeds. If you can answer them at the end, the chapter is yours.
slides.concept: If you can answer these, chapter 2 is yours

slides.title: One chapter, five branches
slides.say: A transaction is the unit of action in Bitcoin: a message telling the network that the owner of certain bitcoins has authorized the transfer of that value to another owner. The new owner can in turn spend the value by creating another transaction, and so on, which gives a chain of ownership. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Transaction, Network and Blockchain.
slides.concept: Five branches - every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: Transactions
slides.say: A transaction is the unit of action in Bitcoin: a message telling the network that the owner of certain bitcoins has authorized the transfer of that value to another owner. The new owner can in turn spend the value by creating another transaction, and so on, which gives a chain of ownership. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Transaction.
slides.concept: Who pays whom, with what, and what it costs

slides.title: Nine pages, and a table of odds
slides.say: On 31 October 2008 a pseudonymous author posted nine pages to a cryptography mailing list. Section 11 does something unusual for a systems paper, because it computes the attacker's odds. For an attacker with ten percent of the power, the paper's table gives about 0.2046 at one confirmation and 0.0002428 at six, and the example group AttackerSuccess reruns both. The sources are Nakamoto's 2008 paper and the announcement on the metzdowd cryptography list.
slides.concept: The paper computes its promises - today we recompute them

slides.title: Alice pays Bob: one transaction, whole
slides.say: A transaction is the unit of action in Bitcoin: a message telling the network that the owner of certain bitcoins has authorized the transfer of that value to another owner. The new owner can in turn spend the value by creating another transaction, and so on, which gives a chain of ownership. A question to think about is this: why must the 100,000 be spent whole rather than split? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Transaction and Input.
slides.concept: A transaction spends whole outputs and makes new ones

slides.title: Your balance is outputs, not an account
slides.say: An unspent transaction output, abbreviated UTXO, is a transaction output that has not yet been used as an input by any later transaction. The glossary defines it as an unspent transaction output that can be spent as an input in a new transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: where does the idea of an 'account balance' live, if not on the chain? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Unspent output and Output.
slides.concept: No accounts anywhere - only unspent outputs your keys can unlock

slides.title: Change comes back to you
slides.say: Making change is the practice of adding to a transaction an output that returns the surplus to the person who is paying. The book explains the need with money in a shop: if you buy a five-dollar item with a twenty-dollar bill you expect fifteen dollars back, and in the same way a transaction input, like a currency note, cannot be partly spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Think about this case: pay a 20-lira coffee with a 50-lira note: where is the change output? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Making change and Transaction fee.
slides.concept: Inputs are spent whole; the difference returns as change

slides.title: Fees price bytes, not value
slides.say: The fee rate is the fee a transaction pays for each unit of the space it takes in a block. Miners do not compare transactions by their total fee alone; they divide the fee by the size of the transaction, as a shopper divides the price of a bag of rice by its weight to find the best deal. A question to think about is this: why does moving 1 BTC cost the same as moving 100? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Fee rate and Transaction size.
slides.concept: You pay for block space - size, not amount

slides.title: The network
slides.say: The Bitcoin network is the set of computers that run the Bitcoin protocol and exchange transactions and blocks with one another. This second branch of the chapter follows Alice's transaction out of her wallet and across that network. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Network.
slides.concept: No postmaster - transactions travel by gossip

slides.title: Five free bitcoins for every visitor
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2010-06-11. In June 2010 there was almost nowhere to buy bitcoin, so a developer in Massachusetts stocked a website with 1,100 of his own coins and gave five to anyone who asked - solving a CAPTCHA was the only price. Thousands of people got their first bitcoin from Gavin Andresen's faucet.
slides.concept: Before exchanges, distribution itself had to be invented

slides.title: A transaction's journey to everyone
slides.say: Transaction propagation is the spread of a signed transaction across the network until it has reached, in practice, everyone who cares, including the miners who may record it. It is the composition of the two previous concepts: the wallet transmits the transaction to some node, and then the gossip rule carries it onward hop by hop. A question to think about is this: what happens if two conflicting spends gossip at once? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Transaction propagation and Mempool.
slides.concept: Four seconds of gossip puts Alice's payment in every mempool

slides.title: Who checks? Everyone who wants to
slides.say: A full node, which the chapter calls a full verification node, is a program that has both the software logic and the data necessary to fully verify the correctness of a new transaction (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: which one is Alice's phone wallet, and what exactly does it trust? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Full node and Lightweight client.
slides.concept: Full nodes verify; light clients trust proofs, not people

slides.title: Watch any transaction live
slides.say: A block explorer is a web application that operates as a Bitcoin search engine: it allows you to search for addresses, transactions and blocks and to see the relationships and flows between them, in the chapter's own words (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why does Bob check his OWN copy rather than trust Alice's screenshot? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Block explorer and Recipient verification.
slides.concept: The ledger is public - explorers are just viewers on it

slides.title: Blockchain and mining
slides.say: The blockchain is the record in which Bitcoin's transactions are finally written down. The chapter calls it the distributed journal of all transactions and, in its opening overview, the consensus blockchain which is the authoritative journal of all transactions (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Blockchain.
slides.concept: How the next page of history gets written

slides.title: Mining: hard to win, instant to verify
slides.say: Proof of work is a piece of data that takes a great deal of computation to find and almost none to check. A question to think about is this: who pays for all the losing tickets? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Proof of work and Sudoku analogy.
slides.concept: Proof-of-work is a lottery whose ticket anyone can check

slides.title: A block, anatomized
slides.say: A block is the unit in which transactions are added to the blockchain. The chapter says that transactions are bundled into blocks, and that blocks have a very small header that must be formed in a very specific way, requiring an enormous amount of computation to get right but only a small amount to verify as correct (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). A question to think about is this: why hash the header only, not the whole megabyte? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Block and Block header.
slides.concept: A header of 80 bytes summarizes everything beneath it

slides.title: One root for a thousand leaves
slides.say: A merkle tree, also called a binary hash tree, is a structure for summarizing and verifying the integrity of large sets of data. The book defines it as a tree constructed by hashing paired data, the leaves, then pairing and hashing the results until a single hash remains, the merkle root, and notes that in Bitcoin the leaves are almost always the transactions of a single block (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). Think about this case: a light client holds only the root. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Merkle tree.
slides.concept: Change any leaf and the root betrays it

slides.title: The coinbase: where new coin enters
slides.say: The coinbase transaction is the special first transaction of every block, by which the miner pays itself. The book's glossary calls it the first transaction in a block, always created by a miner, and the mining chapter adds the distinguishing property: unlike regular transactions the coinbase transaction does not consume unspent outputs as inputs, but has only one input, called the coinbase input, which implicitly contains the block reward (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Coinbase transaction and Block reward.
slides.concept: Every coin in existence began life in a coinbase

slides.title: The day someone printed 184 billion bitcoin
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2010-08-15. On 15 August 2010 block 74,638 contained a transaction paying out about 184,467,440,737 BTC - thousands of times the 21 million cap. Two outputs were so large that, summed as 64-bit integers, they overflowed to a small number and slipped past the checks.
slides.concept: Validation by every node is the immune system - it worked

slides.title: Confirmations: depth, not time
slides.say: A confirmation is a block that commits to a transaction, counted once for the block that contains it and once more for each block built on top. A question to think about is this: why does a reorg of depth 1 happen weekly, depth 6 almost never? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Confirmation and Best blockchain.
slides.concept: Each block on top multiplies the cost of rewriting yours

slides.title: The whitepaper's table, recomputed live
slides.say: This chart is not an illustration: the build ran the whitepaper's section-11 procedure (examples group AttackerSuccess) and drew what it returned; the chapter research record matched the q=0.1 column against the paper to seven decimals. Think about this case: read the 30% line at six blocks. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Probability and Confirmation.
slides.concept: Six confirmations: the attacker's odds drop below 0.03%

slides.title: Zero-conf espresso, six-block house
slides.say: Accepting a small payment unconfirmed is the practice of treating a transaction as paid as soon as it has propagated, without waiting for a block. It is not a rule of Bitcoin but a judgement about risk. A question to think about is this: where would you put a used-car sale on this line? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Small payment acceptance and Unconfirmed transaction.
slides.concept: Match the wait to the stake - that is all 6 blocks means

slides.title: Semantics and practice
slides.say: This branch reads the chapter with the eyes of the course rather than of the book. A transaction chain, as the first branch described it, is a record of what came from what: each output exists because a transaction consumed earlier outputs, and each transaction happened because somebody who held a key authorized it. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Semantics.
slides.concept: The chapter as data, and the chapter on your laptop

slides.title: The chapter as data: triples and provenance
slides.say: A triple is the unit in which these descriptions are written: a subject, a predicate and an object, read as a single sentence. The statement that Alice's transaction used Joe's output is a triple whose subject is the transaction, whose predicate is the relation used and whose object is the output. A question to think about is this: what triple would record Alice's payment to Bob? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Triple and Provenance graph.
slides.concept: The course page you use is built exactly this way

slides.title: Run the chapter at home
slides.say: The last branch of this chapter is about trying things out. The concepts of the earlier branches are all mechanical, which means that a learner can operate them rather than only read about them, and a small number of interactive pages have become the standard way to do that in teaching. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Practice.
slides.concept: Three consoles reproduce the chapter - tonight, on your laptop

slides.title: The chapter in five lines
slides.say: Five lines, one per part. If any feels like a claim rather than a fact, the agenda names the slides that prove it; the course page carries the full text. A question to think about is this: which line would you defend to a sceptic first, and with which slide? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in every section.
slides.concept: If a line feels unproven, its part's slides carry the receipt

slides.title: Where to go from here
slides.say: Everything here is free. Watch one transaction confirm on mempool.space tonight - pick any txid from the latest block - and you will have SEEN this whole chapter happen once. A question to think about is this: who can find Alice-sized fees (about 35 sat/vB) in the current mempool? The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 2, in Practice.
slides.concept: One evening on an explorer replays this whole chapter for free
